# What the central fish would hit

## Short answer

It would hit the sea floor — specifically the coral‑encrusted rock and rubble at the
**base of the left‑hand coral formation, right where it meets the white sandy channel**,
down and to the left of the fish. Impact would come within roughly one body length; it is
not heading out into open water. It would **not** hit the coral wall on the right side of
the frame — that reef is behind its tail, not in front of its head.

## Which fish, and which way it is actually pointing

The large fish at the centre of the frame is a threadfin butterflyfish (*Chaetodon
auriga*): a disc‑shaped fish with a white body crossed by two sets of fine dark chevron
(herringbone) lines, a bright orange‑yellow rear third, and pale fins.

The important and easily misread point is its **direction**. At first glance the bright
orange area with the dark oval, at the upper right of the fish, looks like a head with an
eye, which would make the fish appear to be swimming up and to the right into the reef
wall. It is not the head. Zooming in shows:

- The dark oval is a horizontally elongated **blotch with no eye highlight**, unlike the
  genuine eyes of other fish in the same photo (the small dark striped fish just below
  left of it shows a clear white catchlight). It is the black ocellus/eyespot that
  *C. auriga* carries on the rear edge of its **soft dorsal fin**.
- A very fine dark **filament ("thread")** trails from the tip of that fin up and to the
  right, beyond the body outline, into open water. That trailing thread on the rear edge
  of the dorsal fin is exactly the feature this species is named for, and it marks the
  **back** of the fish.
- Immediately to the right of that fin tip there is a deep **V‑shaped notch**, and beyond
  the notch a separate smooth, pale, fan‑shaped lobe with a dark submarginal line — the
  **caudal (tail) fin**.
- At the opposite, lower‑left end of the fish there is a **white, slightly elongated
  pointed snout**, with a **broad dark bar** immediately behind it running perpendicular to
  the body axis. That is the classic black eye‑band of *C. auriga*.
- The spinous dorsal fin margin runs along the fish's **upper‑left** edge, so the fish's
  back faces up‑and‑left and its belly (the pale cyan area) faces down‑and‑right — exactly
  the posture of an un‑rolled fish pitched nose‑down.

So the fish is **nose‑down, swimming down and to the left**, at roughly **40° below
horizontal** (snout at about pixel (899, 814) in the 1709 × 1080 image, tail/caudal fin up
at about (1015, 712)). The same species and identical posture can be seen in the second,
dimmer butterflyfish at the lower right of the photograph.

## Tracing the path

Projecting that heading forward from the snout, down‑left at about 40°:

1. Within about 40 pixels (roughly a third of the fish's body length) the line enters the
   shadowed, coral‑encrusted rock at the **foot of the left‑hand reef mound** — the
   knobbly, branching coral‑rubble surface that fills the area below and to the left of
   the fish.
2. Continuing, at about 120–160 pixels (a little over one body length) the line reaches
   the **edge of the bright white sand** of the channel floor, at the junction where the
   reef base meets the sand.
3. It passes just **below and behind the small dark, pale‑striped fish** hovering against
   that reef base, and just **below the pale boulder/rock knob** sitting on the sand there
   — so it would clear both of those and strike the ground rather than the other fish.

## Conclusion, stated plainly

- The fish is descending, not climbing.
- Its current path leads into the **seabed at the base of the left‑hand coral head**: first
  the coral‑covered rock and rubble of the reef base, then the white sandy bottom of the
  channel immediately in front of it.
- The obstacle is very close — less than about one and a half body lengths away — so in

- It is **not** on course for the reef wall on the right of the image, nor for the open
  blue water above; both of those lie behind it.
